## Simple explanation

Natural language processing (NLP) is the area of AI concerned with human
language. It includes systems that classify messages, translate text,
answer questions, extract names, and generate responses.

## Technical explanation

NLP combines ideas from linguistics, statistics, and machine learning to
process language data. Tasks range from tokenization and tagging to
sequence modeling, retrieval, and generation. Modern systems often represent
text as tokens and learn contextual representations from large datasets.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Language is a common interface to documents, users, and business processes.
NLP components can search, summarize, classify, or extract information from
text, but engineering them also requires attention to data quality,
evaluation, latency, privacy, and the consequences of errors.

## How it works

A typical NLP workflow cleans or normalizes input, splits text into tokens,
converts tokens into model-compatible representations, and applies a model
for a task. The output may be labels, spans, ranked documents, or generated
text. The right workflow depends on whether the problem is classification,
retrieval, extraction, or generation.

## Practical example

A customer-support tool might classify incoming messages by topic, retrieve
relevant help articles, and draft a response for a human to review. These
are separate NLP capabilities and should each be evaluated for their own
failure modes.

## Common misconceptions

- NLP is broader than large language models; many useful NLP systems use rules, classical models, or specialized neural networks.
- A fluent response is not proof that the system understood the user's intent or gave a correct answer.
- Language systems can inherit biases and gaps from their data and evaluation setup.
